div.head: ECf 11.1 A 6
div.ab: Debet etiam rex omnia rite facere in regno et per iudicium procerum regni. Debet enim ius et iustitia magis regnare in regno quam uoluntas praua; lex est semper quod ius facit; uoluntas uero et uiolentia et uis non est ius.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 635 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page.

This passage is not part of ECf or ECf retr: it is one of the additions of the London collection (Leges Anglorum s. XIII in. Londoniis collectae), which Liebermann prints in smaller type across the page, under ECf retr. 11, 1, and numbers 11, 1 A ff. The dictionary cites it as “ECf 11, 1 A …”, so it is kept with ECf here.

note.seg: vgl. 11, 1 A 8. B 2; dass Adel mitregiere und mitrichte, ohne Willkür der Krone, fordert Lond auch sonst: ebd. S. 54. 99. Die Französische Eidesformel in Anm. c spricht von den Gesetzen, que les gentes de people averont faitz, entzieht also der Krone die Gesetzgebung noch mehr

cf. 11, 1 A 8. B 2; Lond elsewhere too demands that the nobility share in ruling and judging, without arbitrariness on the part of the Crown: ibid. pp. 54. 99. The French form of oath in note c speaks of the laws que les gentes de people averont faitz, so withdraws legislation from the Crown still further

perhaps in contradiction of the tenets of Justinian’s absolutism, which had served the Crown lawyers of Henry II; cf. ibid. p. 42

div.ab: The king ought also to do all things duly in the kingdom and by the judgment of the magnates of the kingdom. For right and justice ought to reign in the kingdom rather than perverse will; law is always what right makes; but will and violence and force are not right.
